findings.text: Swap-out completion entry for a folio already associated with swap cache. It performs accounting for huge and ordinary pages, transitions the folio into writeback, releases its lock, and hands it to the batched device submission path for writing.

Batch accumulator for swap IO that reuses the pending request when the target device matches and the device merge predicate accepts the new folio. It allocates a fresh request on demand, appends the folio extent, and submits eagerly when the request becomes full or when a write targets a synchronous device.

Coalescing requires the incoming folio to belong to the same swap device as the pending batch. Contiguity beyond that is delegated to device-specific logic that compares the new folio against the previous one and the requested direction.
Two size classes are considered merge compatible only when both their per-extent page multiplicity and per-extent object multiplicity agree.
Completion helper for a pending swap read batch. It records the inbound operation, delegates actual submission to the owning device, and detaches the batch and device association from the context.

Top-level attempt to absorb an entire folio into the compressed swap cache. Success means every constituent page was retained in compressed form; any failure triggers cleanup of stale per-page records across the folio range and may schedule background reclaim when the pool reports saturation.
Compressed store expects the folio to arrive locked and already present in swap cache. A disabled global facility bypasses all admission work and proceeds directly to stale-record invalidation.

Admission under the default hierarchy walks from the object owner toward the root. Unlimited ancestors are skipped, an explicit zero limit denies, otherwise recent flushed usage converted to pages is compared against the configured ceiling.

The current compressed pool is selected under a read-side critical section over the pool list, with a reference attempt taken before leaving the section so the returned pointer remains valid or null on failure.
When bookkeeping indicates a pool should exist yet the list yields none, a one-time warning is emitted. Callers must tolerate a null pool and abort the store.
Pool fullness is latched rather than instantaneous. Reaching the ceiling sets the saturated flag and bumps a hit counter; the flag clears only after usage falls back to a lower acceptance watermark.

The ceiling scales with total system memory by a configured percentage, the acceptance watermark scales with that ceiling by a second percentage, and current usage sums allocator-reported totals across all pools under read-side protection.

Per-cgroup compressed-cache reclaim requires writeback permission and an online group, scans a bounded number of reclaim candidates per memory node, and distinguishes empty groups from groups where scanning found nothing reclaimable via distinct negative results.

The node-scoped reclaim walk consumes its visit budget before invoking the callback, then reacts to the outcome by restarting traversal, tallying removals, recycling entries to the tail, skipping, or terminating. Unknown outcomes are treated as fatal.
Traversal holds the locked per-group sublist across callbacks except when the outcome requires dropping the lock and restarting or exiting. Removal outcomes also decrement the node-wide item total.

Per-page worker that obtains metadata storage, attempts compression into the pool allocator, publishes the result into the per-offset lookup structure, displaces any stale predecessor, and on success acquires pool and cgroup references plus usage accounting before linking into reclaim order.

Field initialization and reclaim linkage occur after lookup insertion. Correctness relies on the folio lock to exclude concurrent stores and invalidations, and on absence from reclaim order to exclude writeback until publication completes. Zero-length results remain unlinked.

Compressed-byte charging applies only under the default hierarchy and never to the root group. It expects an allocation-privileged context, charges the object, and updates byte, object, and incompressible counters under read-side protection.

Small object charges first attempt a per-CPU stock under a try-lock; contention or insufficiency falls back to a full charge followed by a stock refill that temporarily permits exceeding the usual byte ceiling to avoid immediate uncharge.

Linkage into the compressed-cache reclaim order resolves the owning group under read-side protection. The operation remains safe across concurrent offlining because late arrivals are reparented to the surviving ancestor.

Insertion is effective only for entries currently detached. Attaching appends to the tail, bumps per-sublist and node-wide totals, and arms the shrinker notification for the owning group only on the empty to nonempty transition.
The shrinker identity accessor has two build configurations, one reporting the registered identifier and another reporting a sentinel that disables per-group notification.

Shrinker notification is recorded only for valid identifiers and non-root groups. The target bit is located by splitting the identifier into a unit index and an offset within that unit, with ordering enforced before the atomic update.
Node-preferred allocation of compressed-entry metadata that may fail and return null under memory pressure.

Compression executes under a per-CPU serialization mutex with a synchronous wait on an asynchronous request. Backing storage is obtained with non-blocking movable high-memory flags, then populated and recorded as handle plus length.

Pages that fail compression or show no size benefit are retained verbatim at full size to preserve writeback ordering when the owner permits writeback; otherwise they are rejected to avoid pure metadata overhead. Distinct counters track poor, failed, and allocation rejections.

Content copy resolves a handle to its location while holding the pool read lock, then pins the backing extent with a read lock that excludes migration before releasing the pool lock and performing the copy, handling both contained and cross-page placements.
Extent read exclusion is implemented as a spin-guarded reader count with dependency-tracking annotations for acquire and release, rather than a conventional reader-writer primitive.

General allocation entry that rejects empty sizes and oversized requests, obtains a handle, and either reuses an existing extent with fullness-group maintenance or creates and links a new extent with page and object accounting plus movable marking. Failures are reported as encoded error pointers.
Size-class reuse, fullness adjustment, and usage accounting occur under the class lock. The lock is released while allocating a fresh extent and reacquired to link and account the new extent.
One build configuration treats movable marking of freshly prepared extents as a no-operation.
The swap IO context pairs a current device pointer with a current batch pointer. The batch itself tracks an array of extents, a used count, and an accumulated byte length.

A compressed pool aggregates a reference count, an allocator instance, per-CPU helper contexts, and list membership. An entry aggregates a backing handle, a stored length, owning pool and swap identity, an optional group reference, a referenced flag, and reclaim linkage.
Reclaim tracking is organized as a top object with per-node totals, per-node per-group sublists each with its own list and count, and a separate per-group per-node shrinker bitmap for notification.

A size class records its per-extent page multiplicity, per-extent object multiplicity, object size, and allocation statistics. An extent lock records a reader count with dependency state for validation.

Insertion into the per-offset tree may report allocation pressure; only the expected no-memory condition is silent while other error codes trigger a one-time warning and are counted as allocation rejections.
Writes targeting devices flagged synchronous are submitted immediately rather than held for further coalescing, serving reclaim-path expectations about prompt writeback clearing.
Byte charging warns when invoked outside the expected privileged allocation context and also warns if charging fails despite that context, since success is required there.

Failed compressed stores release acquired pool and group references, and when saturation was observed they queue background shrinking. Stale predecessor records displaced by successful insertion are freed promptly.
Pool lifetime is managed by a reference count with explicit acquire and conditional try-acquire operations; the latter reports failure as zero without blocking.
